title: Closing the AI Accountability Gap: Defining an End-to-End Framework for Internal Algorithmic Auditing
pub: Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAT* '20), pp. 33-44
author: Inioluwa Deborah Raji · Andrew Smart · Rebecca N. White · Margaret Mitchell · Timnit Gebru · Ben Hutchinson · Jamila Smith-Loud · Daniel Theron · Parker Barnes

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI auditing: Organisational evidence must remain auditable
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s organizational-auditability proposition and materially develops it through SMACTR: an end-to-end lifecycle framework linking documented development decisions, ethical and social-risk assessment, remediation, and deployment. It also treats internal access and external scrutiny as complementary while acknowledging unresolved limits around audit integrity, standardization, selection, and demonstrated effectiveness.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s use-context-specific, risk-based governance premise and materially extends it with SMACTR: a documented, end-to-end internal audit process covering scoping, mapping, artifact collection, testing, reflection and remediation. Although not specific to legal work or jagged legal capability, it provides a concrete operating model for pre-deployment testing, organizational accountability and context-sensitive oversight.

kp.k: Internal auditing shifts accountability toward prevention
kp.d: Raji and colleagues propose internal algorithmic audits throughout AI development to anticipate harms before deployment, guide mitigation and support decisions not to proceed when risks outweigh benefits. This is a cross-domain AI governance framework, not evidence about changes in legal employment or legal services.

kp.k: Ethical compliance differs from technical reliability
kp.d: The authors locate accountability in organizations rather than algorithms and argue that technical reliability does not establish ethical acceptability. Ethical governance should evaluate social benefits and values rather than rely exclusively on accuracy, profitability or conventional quality assurance.

kp.k: Organizational principles supply provisional audit standards
kp.d: The paper acknowledges criticism that AI principles are vague and lack accountability mechanisms. In the absence of universal formal standards, the authors nevertheless propose treating declared organizational principles as objectives against which development decisions and risks can be assessed, translating ethical commitments into operational practice.

kp.d: The authors argue that external audits are constrained by limited access to training data, intermediate models and internal processes. Internal auditors can investigate otherwise inaccessible sources of risk and recommend organizational changes. Their documentation can also support third-party auditing and communication with end users; internal auditing is presented as complementary to external accountability.

kp.k: Audit integrity depends on trustworthy procedures
kp.d: Drawing on tax compliance and financial auditing, the authors argue that a fair, thorough and established methodology helps secure acceptance of findings. Auditors should themselves follow ethical standards and transparent procedures, because perceived dishonesty or opacity can cause audited organizations to dismiss results.

kp.k: Safety-critical industries provide transferable audit practices
kp.d: The paper draws on aerospace checklists, traceability and Failure Modes and Effects Analysis, medical-device design controls and design history files, and financial auditing infrastructure. These are proposed foundations for AI governance rather than demonstrated results of applying SMACTR. Checklists should avoid mechanical box-ticking, and the authors state that, to their knowledge, FMEA had not been applied to ethical risks in production-scale AI.

kp.k: AI development creates distinctive auditability challenges
kp.d: Rapid iterative development, coupled sociotechnical systems, data entanglement, incomplete requirements and general-purpose applications complicate auditing. The authors propose explicit documentation of purpose, data and models to identify hazards earlier, while recognizing that risk-based governance alone may miss profound technological impacts. Auditors may need to help engineering teams reconstruct missing documentation.

kp.k: SMACTR organizes five stages around documentary evidence
kp.d: The proposed framework comprises Scoping, Mapping, Artifact Collection, Testing and Reflection, each producing documentation for an overall audit report. Scoping establishes ethical objectives and intended impacts; mapping identifies stakeholders and processes; collection assembles development records; testing probes prioritized risks; reflection translates findings into risk assessments and recommendations. The paper illustrates the framework through fictional consulting projects, not an empirical implementation study.

kp.k: Metrics cannot settle ethical acceptability alone
kp.d: The authors warn that conventional performance metrics can conceal fairness concerns and abstraction errors. Metrics must be interpreted within engineering and social contexts, while interviews should identify what measurements exclude. Choosing whether to prioritize false positives or false negatives is a value judgment that requires explicit organizational, team or engineer commitments.

kp.k: Documentation creates traceability across development decisions
kp.d: The framework recommends design checklists, datasheets and model cards to record data provenance, intended uses, assumptions, performance characteristics and limitations. An algorithmic design history file should collect development and audit records, enabling reconstruction of key decisions. A summary report then consolidates findings for review against ethical objectives and engineering requirements.

kp.k: Remediation extends beyond improving model performance
kp.d: In the fictional smile-detection example, potential responses include more diverse training data, user consent, disabling the automated trigger by default and privacy assurances. The hypothetical child-abuse screening project could instead be delayed or cancelled. These examples demonstrate that audit responses may involve product design and deployment decisions, not merely model adjustment. The authors acknowledge that acceptable ethical performance thresholds remain difficult to define.

kp.k: Internal audits require broader checks and balances
kp.d: The authors acknowledge that internal auditors share organizational interests with those they audit, complicating independence and creating a risk of reputation management. They therefore position internal auditing as one element of a wider accountability system. They also leave the selection of which systems require audits outside the framework's scope and allow lighter or fuller implementations depending on context and desired scrutiny.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Raji, Smart and co-authors argue that large-scale AI deployment creates social and ethical risks that technical reliability checks alone do not address.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain paper about AI development and organizational accountability, not a prediction about legal services or legal employment. The authors describe rapidly expanding deployment by corporations, nonprofits and governments, with systems potentially replicating or amplifying existing social biases. They distinguish ethical compliance from technical accuracy, reliability and profitability, arguing for governance directed specifically at social impacts. They also argue that developers' assumptions and values become embedded in algorithms, while isolated performance metrics can obscure fairness problems and deployment-context risks.

pts.k: The authors propose lifecycle-wide internal auditing as a way to anticipate harms, guide mitigation and support decisions not to deploy risky AI.
pts.d: The proposed SMACTR framework comprises Scoping, Mapping, Artifact Collection, Testing and Reflection. The authors argue that internal access to development processes, training data, intermediate models and personnel can expose risks unavailable to outside investigators. Documentation, stakeholder interviews, social impact assessment, failure-mode analysis and adversarial testing are intended to make ethical concerns actionable before launch. Resulting recommendations may change training data, product design, consent mechanisms or deployment decisions, including delaying or cancelling a project. These are proposed capabilities and illustrative outcomes, rather than measured effects of an implemented SMACTR program.

pts.k: The authors claim audit documentation can improve traceability, support organizational changes and facilitate external scrutiny.
pts.d: The framework's documentation is intended to connect system purposes, development choices, testing, ethical expectations and remediation. An algorithmic design history file would preserve the basis for reconstructing development decisions, with a summary report consolidating findings for review. Internal audits are presented as complements to external accountability, not substitutes: documentation can support third-party auditing and communication, while findings can motivate changes to engineering processes. The authors also expect the process to promote ethical awareness among employees.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists principally of prior research, auditing precedents from other industries and hypothetical demonstrations, rather than an empirical evaluation of SMACTR.
pts.d: The authors cite external AI audits, including Gender Shades, as evidence of demographic performance disparities and cite research on predictive policing, child welfare and sociotechnical risks. They draw on aerospace checklists, traceability and failure-mode analysis; medical-device design controls and design history files; financial-audit infrastructure; and tax-compliance research on procedural justice. These precedents motivate the framework but are not reported measurements of its effectiveness in AI development. Company X, its child-abuse screening project and its smile-detection client are explicitly hypothetical. The worked example uses model-card and datasheet approaches and cited dataset research; the paper does not report a real-company trial establishing reduced harms, improved compliance or quantified audit benefits.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2020 proposal emphasizes intervention throughout development and before deployment, with continued attention after launch; it gives no dated adoption forecast.
pts.d: The authors present a prospective governance mechanism rather than a schedule for industry transformation. Auditing should begin with intended use, ethical principles and social context, then inform testing and deployment decisions. Post-launch testing and updated risk analysis are also contemplated. Audit scope and intensity depend on the use case, organization, industry and available resources. The framework assumes an audit has already been deemed necessary; deciding which systems require auditing is outside its principal scope. Its usefulness depends on access to information and collaborators, adequate documentation, context-sensitive testing and decision-makers able to respond. The authors acknowledge that acceptable ethical-risk thresholds remain difficult to specify, internal auditors share organizational interests, and risk assessment cannot reliably anticipate every sociotechnical consequence.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The authors identify impacts on AI-producing organizations, auditors and external reviewers, as well as unequal harms to affected communities.
pts.d: Engineering and product teams would participate in documentation, interviews, testing and remediation; dedicated internal auditors would coordinate scrutiny; leadership would make informed deployment decisions; and external reviewers could use the resulting records. The authors emphasize inclusion of domain experts and marginalized groups to surface assumptions that developers may miss. Their hypothetical child-welfare example illustrates risks to children, families and screening staff from false positives and false negatives. The smile-detection example illustrates exclusion of users whose expressions differ because of autism, cultural norms or photographic preferences, alongside biometric privacy concerns. More broadly, the authors argue that people already experiencing structural vulnerability disproportionately bear AI harms. These are public-impact and governance claims, not claims about law-firm market segments or access to legal representation.
